> **A note on evaluation.** The code in this vignette is shown for illustration
> and is **not executed** when the vignette is built, so no figures or printed
> output are embedded here. Every chunk runs as-is against the bundled
> `demo_eres` dataset; copy them into an interactive session to reproduce the
> diagnostics locally.

## 1  A diagnostic question, not an inferential one

A fitted logistic model is only as trustworthy as the picture it paints. After a
stepwise covariate search settles on body weight as a predictor of the binary
safety endpoint, the natural next question is diagnostic rather than inferential:
does the model's predicted event probability actually track the observed rates we
see in the data, stratum by stratum? In this vignette we fit an exposure–safety
logistic model to the bundled `demo_eres` cohort, attach human-readable weight
labels through a variable specification, and compare predicted probability curves
against binned observed event rates across weight strata. The emphasis is on
getting the comparison *right* — ensuring the axis and bin labels reflect the
original weight scale, so that "≤ 62" and "> 80" mean exactly what a clinician
expects, whether we use a handful of bins or many.

This vignette is the logistic-regression companion to
`vignette("cox-covariate-effect-plots", package = "erSCM")`. It uses the same
cohort and the same weight-stratification idea so the two diagnostics read in
parallel.

## 2  Setup

```{r load}
library(erSCM)
data("demo_eres")

demo_eres <- demo_eres |>
  dplyr::mutate(SEX = as.factor(SEX))
```

As on the Cox side, variable metadata is declared once and reused for the plot
labels.

```{r var-spec}
my_spec <- parse_var_spec(c(
  CMAXss = "Cmax,ss (ng/mL)",
  WT     = "Body Weight (kg)",
  AGE    = "Age (years)",
  SEX    = "Sex"
))
```

## 3  Fit the logistic SCM

```{r fit-glm}
lr_fit <- scm_glm(
  eres_data          = demo_eres,
  exposure_vars      = "CMAXss",
  covariates         = c("WT", "AGE", "SEX"),
  dv_col             = "sim_status",
  significance_level = c(0.05, 0.01),
  var_spec           = my_spec,
  center             = TRUE
)
```

## 4  Predicted probability vs. observed rates by weight

`plot_logistic_terms()` draws the smooth predicted-probability curve with a
confidence ribbon and overlays binned observed event rates. The binning follows
the same quantile logic used on the Cox side, so the two vignettes describe the
weight axis identically.

```{r plot-glm-default}
plot_logistic_terms(lr_fit, "WT")
```

The binned observed points carry back-transformed weight labels on the original
scale. Those labels are produced from a small, explicit vocabulary of
transformations — none, centred, median-scaled, median-scaled-and-centred, and
log-transformed — and the function stops with a clear error rather than emitting a
mislabelled axis if it is ever handed an unrecognised transform. In practice this
means "≤ 62" and "> 80" always denote kilograms, never a centred or scaled proxy.

## 5  Finer bins and the raw components

As with the Cox term plot, increasing `n_bins` keeps the labels on the original
scale and keeps each observed point aligned with the interval it summarises.

```{r plot-glm-fine, fig.height = 6}
plot_logistic_terms(lr_fit, "WT", n_bins = 12)
```

Set `plot = FALSE` to retrieve the prediction grid and the binned observations as
tibbles, ready for bespoke plotting or tabulation.

```{r plot-glm-data}
glm_parts <- plot_logistic_terms(lr_fit, "WT", plot = FALSE)
head(glm_parts$predictions)
head(glm_parts$observed)
```

## 6  Non-linear covariate forms via the fitting API

Body weight need not enter linearly. The fractional-polynomial and spline
machinery is exposed through the `scm_glm()` fitting arguments, so a non-linear
weight effect is requested at fit time and then visualised with the same term
plot. The candidate powers for the fractional polynomial are validated against
the supported set `c(-2, -1, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1, 2, 3)`, and an out-of-set power is
rejected rather than silently coerced.

```{r fit-glm-nonlinear}
lr_fit_nl <- scm_glm(
  eres_data          = demo_eres,
  exposure_vars      = "CMAXss",
  covariates         = c("WT", "AGE"),
  dv_col             = "sim_status",
  significance_level = c(0.05, 0.01),
  var_spec           = my_spec,
  center             = TRUE,
  nonlinear          = list(WT = c("linear", "log", "fp2")),
  linearity_alpha    = 0.05,
  fp_powers          = c(-2, -1, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1, 2, 3)
)
```

`plot_nonlinear_effect()` renders the selected functional form for `WT`; see
`vignette("nonlinear-transformations", package = "erSCM")` for the full treatment
of the non-linear search.

```{r plot-glm-nonlinear}
plot_nonlinear_effect(lr_fit_nl, "WT", scale = "link", rug = TRUE)
```

## 7  A note on quiet internals

As on the Cox side, the grouped summaries and joins that build these diagnostics
are silent by construction: `plot_logistic_terms()` does not print `dplyr`
"joining by" messages or grouped-output notes, so it is safe to embed in reports
and loops.
